1:00–2:00 · Set the purpose

Today’s One-Hour Route

00–15
Compare the evidence

Separate repeat-content familiarity from pacing, precision, and interface habits.

15–30
Repair one ELA decision

Keep a word’s effect inside its sentence; make evidence earn the claim.

11:00–13:00 · Find the first wrong decision

Name the Repair, Not the Feeling

01

Concept

Could you set up the relationship without help?

If not, repair the model.

02

Execution

Was the setup sound but a sign, unit, or count lost?

Repair one visible checking step.

03

Interface / time

Was the written result not entered, or was the item abandoned under pressure?

Repair the commit routine.

“Careless” is a conclusion only after the correct method can be reconstructed. A wrong response alone does not identify its cause.

15:00–17:00 · Final ELA fix

Make the Sentence Set the Boundary

A compact meaning test

  1. Who or what does the word describe?
  2. What neutral phrase could replace it?
  3. What changes when the original word returns?
  4. Does your claim stay inside the cited text?

Why this works

A topic may be alarming while a particular sentence describes a machine, an object, or an action—not the author’s prediction.

The scope trap

Which would require more evidence: “this object seems vulnerable” or “the entire problem cannot be solved”?

Level 1 Locate   Level 2 Connect   Level 3 Discriminate   Level 4 Transfer

Instructional levels match the supplied deck’s four-tier system; they are not CAT difficulty estimates. Repair lens informed by Form B Q11.
17:00–20:00 · Read before choosing

A Word’s Effect Is Not Its Topic

Original transfer text · device-processing setting

Beyond the sorting table, retired tablets advanced in a silent line. A steel gate closed behind each one. The next machine waited, indifferent to the bright screens it would reduce to fragments.

Read once for the scene. Read again for what the description makes you notice.

E1Level 2

What does “indifferent” contribute to the portrayal of the machine?

Before committing: which claims need facts that the paragraph never supplies?

Original classroom transfer item inspired by the decision tested in supplied Form B Q11; not a reproduction of its passage or choices. No response is graded.
20:00–22:00 · Read the evidence

Whose Standard? Whose Preference?

“Impressions of an Indian Childhood” · Zitkala-Sa

4It took many trials before I learned how to knot my sinew thread on the point of my finger, as I saw her do. Then the next difficulty was in keeping my thread stiffly twisted, so that I could easily string my beads upon it. My mother required of me original designs for my lessons in beading. At first I frequently ensnared many a sunny hour into working a long design. Soon I learned from self-inflicted punishment to refrain from drawing complex patterns, for I had to finish whatever I began.

Continue · passage numbering retained

5After some experience I usually drew easy and simple crosses and squares. These were some of the set forms. My original designs were not always symmetrical nor sufficiently characteristic, two faults with which my mother had little patience. The quietness of her oversight made me feel strongly responsible and dependent upon my own judgment. She treated me as a dignified little individual as long as I was on my good behavior; and how humiliated I was when some boldness of mine drew forth a rebuke from her!

Sinew: strong animal tissue used as thread. Mark a preference, a standard, and a consequence. Do not treat the narrator’s feelings as the mother’s thoughts.

Public-domain text explicitly identified as such in supplied Form B, printed pages 36–37. Excerpts preserve the supplied wording.
22:00–25:00 · Evidence must match the relationship

A Shared Activity Can Hide Different Aims

E2 · Q55 transferLevel 3

How can you demonstrate a difference between the child’s approach to design and the mother’s expectations?

You need evidence for both sides. A detail about a shared technique may not establish a difference.

The counterfactual check

If the child and mother wanted exactly the same thing, which textual detail would become difficult to explain?

Based on supplied Form B Q55 and the public-domain passage. Question wording and diagram are original; no final claim is supplied.
25:00–28:00 · Make the pivot do work

Do Not Confuse Setting with Structure

Public-domain passage · paragraph 7, opening

Always after these confining lessons I was wild with surplus spirits, and found joyous relief in running loose in the open again. Many a summer afternoon a party of four or five of my playmates roamed over the hills with me. We each carried a light sharpened rod about four feet long, with which we pried up certain sweet roots.

Compare this opening with paragraphs 4–5. You may return to those slides during discussion.

E3 · Q56 transferLevel 3

Describe the change introduced by the first sentence using two precise nouns—not merely “inside” and “outside.”

Would a claim about all reservation life exceed the evidence? What smaller contrast can this sentence actually establish?

Public-domain excerpt from supplied Form B; instructional transfer from Q56. Diagram-free layout keeps the passage’s own contrast central.

Check Meaning Without Broadening It

E4Level 4

Our final passage-set check

State your ELA repair in one sentence: “When a choice sounds plausible, I will first check ______.”
CAT rule: passage-set responses may be revised only before submitting that set. Source: NYCPS preparation guidance, checked November 2, 2026.

Interrogate the boundary

Does the word “more” remove the boundary value? Can one game belong to two different goal-count rows?

Why a second route helps

The event and its complement partition the whole table. Can two independently built calculations verify the same result?

Data and underlying task: supplied Form B Q103. Report records this item as missed. No numerical result is displayed or stored.
32:00–35:00 · Distinguishable roles

A Pair Is Not Just Two Numbers

M2 · Form B Q100Level 2

A red spinner and a blue spinner each have four equal sections labeled 1–4. Each is spun once.

Find the probability that the product of the two numbers is 4.

List the event first. Then count the full sample space using the same outcome definition.

Underlying task: supplied Form B Q100. Redrawn blank outcome grid; no favorable cells or computed products are marked.
35:00–39:00 · Count groups, not arrangements

Does Swapping People Create Anything New?

M3 · Form B Q98Level 3

A company has six summer workers, two of whom are male. It will hire a group of three permanent employees.

How many possible groups contain exactly one male worker?

Two possible routes

Could a systematic list expose duplicates? Could a choose-then-combine model count the same objects more efficiently?

Facts and task: supplied Form B Q98. Worker identifiers and diagram are original. No count or completed inventory is supplied.
39:00–42:00 · Explain the mechanism

Keep One Definition of “Outcome”

Spinner pair

The red and blue spinners retain different roles.

Employee group

The selected employees receive no distinct roles.

A numerator that counts groups cannot sit over a denominator that counts ordered arrangements. First make the counted objects match.

An elegant check: describe one object counted by the numerator and one counted by the denominator. Do they have the same structure?

42:00–45:00 · Cold transfer and reset

Turn the Group Count into a Probability

M4 · Q98 extensionLevel 4

Use the same six workers. Suppose every three-person group is equally likely to be chosen.

What is the probability that the selected group contains exactly one male worker?

Can a second model audit the first?

If you model sequential draws instead, what must change after a worker is selected? How will you account for different possible positions of the male worker?

Before committing

Does the result fit the range of a probability? Have all and only the qualifying groups been counted?

Pause for one breath. State your counting rule without using a number. Then state the check you will repeat on test day.

Original extension of supplied Form B Q98. Added equal-likelihood assumption is explicit. This is an instructional transfer, not an official CAT item.
45:00–47:00 · Strategy lock begins

Know Exactly What “Move On” Means

Math

Respond before advancing. After advancing, you cannot return to that item.

The check happens before Next.

ELA passage set

Review and revise within the current set. After submitting the set, you cannot return to it.

The final check happens before submitting the set.

ELA standalone

After advancing, you cannot return to the previous standalone item.

Do not plan a later cleanup pass.

A section is also a boundary

Complete the first subject before moving to the second. Once a subject is submitted, you cannot return to it.

Official basis: NYCPS preparation guidance and NYC Guide to the SHSAT for 2027 Admissions, “Learn About the Test.” Checked November 2, 2026.
47:00–50:00 · Choose from observed performance

Lock an Order You Have Rehearsed

Standard-time total: 180 minutes.

What evidence decides the order?

Which order preserved accuracy without forcing a rushed second subject? Does the log support the choice, or does the choice merely feel safer?

No unsupported last-minute experiment

Keep the rehearsed order unless actual comparison data justifies a change. “Math first” is not an automatic rule.

Official standard administration: 50 ELA items, 50 math items, 180 minutes. Budget and order are personalized coaching choices, not mandated section limits.
50:00–52:00 · Write the checkpoint, not a wish

Make the Clock Trigger a Decision

Math checkpoint

The study plan proposes Q25 at or under 45 minutes used in math. Check that this fits the locked section budget.

ELA checkpoint

Use the start of passage block 4 as the plan’s checkpoint. Set the target from the actual rehearsal; passage lengths may vary.

Translate before test day

If the display shows time remaining, can you recognize your checkpoint immediately? Is your checkpoint measured from the start of the subject or the entire test?

Source: CATSHSATplan.md, Session 15 and math pacing targets. These are coaching checkpoints, not official section deadlines.
52:00–54:00 · Protect the next item

A Bail-Out Still Requires a Response

2½ minutes

The plan’s upper guardrail for an item—not an entitlement to spend that long on every item.

If the approach is stalled, use a valid elimination or estimate, select the most defensible response, and advance.

Ask before time disappears

  1. Am I making a new, useful step?
  2. Could a representation or estimate unlock it?
  3. What can I rule out with certainty?
  4. Have I entered a response before moving on?
2.5-minute rule: supplied study plan. Official CAT navigation does not permit returning to math or completed standalone items. Never interpret “bail” as “skip and return.”
54:00–56:00 · Rehearse aloud

Use Two Short Routines, Not Pep Talks

Passage 1: careful speed

  1. Take one breath before reading.
  2. Give each paragraph a short job label.
  3. State the passage’s purpose tentatively.
  4. Answer from the relevant text.
  5. Check the current set before submitting.

Math Q25: ten-second reset

  1. Commit the current response.
  2. Take one breath.
  3. Read the next stem twice.
  4. Mark exactly what is asked.
  5. Solve, estimate-check, enter, commit.

The adaptive mindset

Do not use a question’s apparent difficulty to guess your score. Your task is to interpret this item accurately, make one useful check, and continue.

Routines adapted from CATSHSATplan.md. The deck does not simulate adaptive routing or estimate CAT ability.
56:00–58:00 · Check what the screen records

Your Scratch Work Is Not Your Entry

Before every commit

One real entry rehearsal

Use your M4 work. Write the requested probability here, then compare the entry with your scratch paper.

This text field is not the official equation editor. Follow the live item’s directions and practiced input tools.

NYCPS guide: scratch-paper work is not counted; responses must be entered on screen. Official math tools include an equation editor. No calculator.
58:00–60:00 · Read it back, then lock it

One Card. No New Strategy Changes.

Josephine’s strategy card

Order: Not yet locked
Budget: Math ___ min · ELA ___ min
Math Q25: Set target and action
ELA block 4: Set target and action
Stalled item: Use the 2.5-minute guardrail; enter a defensible response; move on.
Passage 1: Breath · paragraph jobs · purpose · evidence · set review.
Math reset: Breath · reread · mark the ask · solve · estimate · enter.
Entry: Check required count, form, sign, and on-screen record.
Commit: Check before the relevant boundary. Do not plan to return.

Without looking, state your order, both checkpoints, bail-out action, reset, warm-up, and entry rule.

Which sentence tells you what to do when the clock is late—not merely when it is on time?
